issues.legal_issue: A party asserting a custom that differs from Hindu law must prove the custom before it governs succession.
material_facts: The parties were Hindus in Punjab and the claim concerned succession.
The claimant relied on a customary rule said to differ from Hindu law.
issues.conclusion: Hindu law applies in the first instance, and a party asserting a different custom must prove both that the custom applies and what its terms are. The proof required may be less for a general, well-recognised custom than for a special custom.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Punjab Laws Act, 1872 makes Hindu law the initial rule for Hindus, subject to an applicable custom. The burden to establish a custom rests on the party asserting it, as stated in Daya Ram v. Sohel Singh, approved in Abdul Hussein Khan v. Bibi Sona Dero and followed in Ujagar Singh v. Mst. Jeo.

predicates.punjab_inheritance_dispute: The dispute concerns inheritance among parties governed by the law applicable in Punjab.
predicates.custom_claimed_to_displace_personal_law: A party relies on a customary rule that differs from the otherwise applicable personal law.

issues.definition: When an inheritance dispute governed by Punjab law involves a claimed departure from personal law, the custom governs only if the party relying on it proves it.

issues.legal_issue: An adopted son does not retain a right under Hindu law to inherit in his natural family unless the adoption is in the form that preserves rights in both families.
material_facts: The claimant was adopted into another family before his natural father died.
The claimant did not assert that the adoption was in the dvyamushyayana form.
The claim concerned property in the claimant’s natural family.
issues.conclusion: Under Hindu law, the claimant had no right to succeed to the property in his natural family after the adoption.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Hindu law as the initial rule under section 5 of the Punjab Laws Act, 1872. It held that an adoption in the dvyamushyayana form was the exception that could preserve rights in the natural family; that form was not asserted in this case.

predicates.natural_family_inheritance_claim: An adopted person claims inheritance in the family into which the person was born.
predicates.adopted_into_another_family: The person was adopted into a family other than the natural family.
predicates.adoption_does_not_preserve_rights_in_bot: The adoption was not of a form that preserves inheritance rights in both families.

issues.definition: An adopted person claiming inheritance in the natural family has no such right under Hindu law when the adoption was into another family and did not preserve rights in both families.

issues.legal_issue: Under the customary law applied to Brahmins and Khatris in the Amritsar district, an adopted person claiming a natural grandparent’s estate through representation is excluded when the represented position includes another son in the natural family.
material_facts: The claimant was a Brahmin from the Amritsar district and had been adopted into another family.
He claimed a share of his natural grandfather’s estate through his natural father, who had died before the grandfather.
Another son of the grandfather was alive.
The customary materials showed that an adopted son could succeed to his natural father’s property if there was no other son, but could not succeed if there was another son.
The claimant argued that he could represent his father without being treated as a son alongside the other son for purposes of the custom.
issues.conclusion: The claimant could not inherit the natural grandfather’s property. Because representation had to be fully applied, he was treated as standing in his father’s place; the other son in the natural family therefore excluded him under the custom.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Punjab Laws Act, 1872 makes an established custom applicable in place of Hindu law. The Court derived the relevant Amritsar custom for Brahmins and Khatris from the customary-law materials, including Rattigan’s Digest, paragraph 48, and the district compilations. It also considered the treatment of riwaj-i-am entries in Jai Kaur v. Sher Singh and Mt. Subhani v. Nawab. The principle of representation must be fully worked out: a claimant who succeeds as though standing in a predeceased parent’s place is treated as that parent for the relevant succession, including the effect of another son in the family.

predicates.customary_inheritance_dispute: The succession claim is governed by a proved custom rather than the ordinary personal-law rule.
predicates.adopted_person_claims_grandparent_estate: An adopted person claims a natural grandparent’s estate by representing a natural parent who died before the grandparent.
predicates.represented_position_has_another_natural: Treating the claimant as standing in the predeceased parent’s place would leave another son in the relevant natural-family succession position.

issues.definition: An adopted person claiming a natural grandparent’s estate through a predeceased natural parent is excluded when full application of representation places another son in the natural-family succession position.
